 After a rookie year derailed by injury, Watkins is getting his chance with the receiver-depleted 49ers. On Sunday, he had his latest sign of progress — his first career touchdown. Thearon W. Henderson / Getty Images 
 By Marcus Thompson II Nov. 9, 2026 Updated Share article 28 SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Before the snap on third-and-3 from the 37, Brock Purdy watched Las Vegas Raiders safety Jeremy Chinn creep to the line of scrimmage and then shadow San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey to the right flat. Cornerback Taron Johnson rotated back to play free safety. Receiver Jacob Cowing ran a crossing route, luring Johnson with him toward the right sideline.
 And Purdy saw a window for Jordan Watkins.
 Advertisement
 The Raiders abandoned the middle of the field, which left the 49ers’ second-year receiver in one-on-one coverage on the left. Watkins’ skinny post route put him inside of Las Vegas cornerback Hezekiah Masses, and Purdy’s pass led Watkins to the middle of the field. The 6-foot-1 Masses had the height advantage. But the 5-11 Watkins had hunger on his side, and the trust of his MVP-caliber quarterback.
 During training camp and OTAs, Watkins had a knack for catching jump balls. So Purdy gave him one when it mattered most.
 “I was like, ‘Alright, this is a great opportunity for J-Wat to go make a play,'” Purdy said. “And he did. Came down with it.”
 With Masses on his back, Watkins snatched the ball out of the air and clutched it like a dream. Not just his own.
 He gripped tighter as he collided with the ground. A 37-yard touchdown, punctuating the 49ers’ 38-17 win Sunday . Redemption from a missed moment last game. The statement he’d waited a season and a half to make.
 Top Plays from Raiders @ 49ers “I was making sure that ball wasn’t going to move on that one,” Watkins said. “I promise you that.”
 Frustration could’ve taken up residence in Watkins. Calf and ankle injuries derailed his rookie season. He’s struggled to find footing in an offense notoriously difficult for young players. And even though injuries thinned out the 49ers’ wide receiver room, the balls still weren’t coming his way. Harvest still hadn’t arrived.
 Watching from the sidelines, praying for snaps, waiting for opportunities, such can wreak havoc on a player’s mind. Motivation becomes harder to sustain, positivity more elusive, purpose increasingly clouded.
 But for most of his career — from Butler Traditional High School in Louisville, to the SEC with Ole Miss, to the 138th pick of the 2025 NFL Draft — Watkins’ purpose remained clear. Injections of positivity came frequently. His motivation kept growing.
 That’s what happens in preadolescence.
 Advertisement
 “My little sister,” Watkins said of his motivation. “She’s very similar to me. She’s very outgoing. She’s tall. She’s one of a kind for sure, I’ll tell you that much. And she looks up to me. She looks up to me a lot.”
 Her name is Abrielle. She’s 12 now, a promising softball player who wears the No. 11 because it was her big brother’s number in college. She’s playing up in age on her travel ball team, so now they’re both fighting to prove themselves.
 Jordan Watkins (left), with sister Abrielle and brother Elijah. (Courtesy of the Watkins family) Her admiration comes with responsibility for Watkins. But his smile came easier with her. His sacrifices lost a bit of their sting. Because Abrielle was worth it. While pursuing his passion, he also revealed to his little sister how to pursue hers. How to endure when things don’t go her way. How to keep believing when the results don’t quite reward the effort.
 His childhood gave him enough experience with such to learn this lesson multiple times over. So Watkins kept working. Kept believing. His time would come.
 Sunday, it did. Seemingly from the heavens, in the form of a Purdy pass that sought out Watkins like a special delivery. It carried so much more weight than six points. But validation.
 His first career touchdown and his four catches for 86 yards offered the strongest evidence yet of his emergence. The 24-year-old who just wanted a chance cashed it in upon arrival.
 Watkins’ breakout performance comes at a particularly crucial time. The 49ers, desperate at wide receiver, need reliable weapons for Purdy. Two days after Brandon Aiyuk showed up looking to get reinstated , underscoring the chaos of San Francisco’s receiver situation, Watkins’ steadiness and perseverance redecorated the receiving corps.
 Once an afterthought, he looked a lot like an answer to the 49ers’ prayers on Sunday. And even more like Abrielle’s big brother.
 Advertisement
 “Jordan, man,” left tackle Trent Williams said, “his maturation is showing right now in front of our eyes. Every week they put more and more on his plate. And every week he shows that he can handle it.”
 This moment feels like destiny now. His teammates’ delight suggested Watkins’ breakthrough felt overdue.
 The 49ers’ first pick in this year’s draft, De’Zhaun Stribling, injured his ankle in Week 1 and, after surgery, was placed on injured reserve . Ricky Pearsall, the 49ers’ first-round pick in 2024, injured his knee in Week 4 last year and missed eight games. He had surgery on the knee this offseason and will miss the entire season .
 In Week 5, Deebo Samuel pulled his hamstring in Seattle. Sunday was his third missed game. Mike Evans, who’s emerged as the 49ers’ best receiver, missed his second consecutive game with rib and Achilles injuries.
 The 49ers reportedly tried to get Jauan Jennings back from Minnesota, but he nixed that deal. They’ve added Dante Pettis, Brandin Cooks and KhaDarel Hodge, trying to make up for the NFL-high 34 games missed by their receivers.
 Meanwhile, opportunity remained scarce for Watkins. He grew concerned enough to approach head coach Kyle Shanahan, searching for answers about how to get on the field.
 “That was kind of — I wouldn’t say rock bottom,” Watkins said. “But almost for me.”
 The question wasn’t whether he belonged, but when he could prove it.
 Jordan Watkins hauls in a 37-yard touchdown pass from Brock Purdy late in the 49ers’ win Sunday over the Raiders. It was his first career touchdown. (Brooke Sutton / Getty Images) This isn’t the first time football required Watkins to overcome. As a teenager, his anger threatened to take away football. Suspensions made him ineligible at his public high school, forcing his family to find another way.
 His mother and stepfather scraped together enough money to enroll him in a private school.
 “They had to sacrifice everything just so I could play football,” Watkins told The Athletic in a 2024 profile . “I messed things up by being spiteful, but I saw what they were trying to do for me.”
 Watkins had to do something harder: confront the resentment that shaped his behavior.
 Advertisement
 He was 8 years old when he watched police take away his mother, Paula Baker. She battled addiction and spent 18 months incarcerated. He didn’t see her for nearly two years. His father had never been a steady presence.
 The reunion with mom wasn’t easy after she regained custody. He struggled with resentment. Abrielle kept him tethered to the joy life tried to bury.
 Watkins eventually embraced therapy. His mother eventually built a life in recovery. They repaired their relationship, and he developed into a college prospect. He’d already learned how a difficult beginning didn’t have to dictate the ending.
 A lesson he needed when a high ankle sprain impacted his first NFL preseason. Then a calf strain derailed his rookie campaign.
 Making up for lost reps and undeveloped chemistry requires mental fortitude. It’s all uphill climbing. Snaps are currency in football, and Watkins’ portfolio was bare.
 “Last year he got kind of screwed,” tight end George Kittle said. “He had a little calf thing so he missed some time. Then it’s hard to get a rhythm when you’re the rookie who’s just trying to find the field.”
 Which teams could make moves as the NFL trade deadline approaches? Jonathan Jones So imagine Watkins landing on the inactive list for the season opener in Australia. Then imagine when his Week 7 touchdown in Atlanta — a 23-yard connection where Watkins leaped for the catch and niftily tapped both feet in bounds — got wiped away because he didn’t maintain control of the ball when he crashed to the turf. And the 49ers lost.
 Watkins lived with that through the bye week. But his recent production showed progress. He made a third-down catch against Washington on Monday Night Football. He caught three passes for 56 yards against Atlanta.
 Gradual headway, but headway nonetheless.
 “I feel like over these last couple of weeks, you can see it,” Watkins said of his increased involvement in the offense. “Just seeing the trust from Kyle starting to grow, I’m super grateful.”
 Advertisement
 Watkins knows disappointment. Hardship. Doubt. But he always had his little sister to replenish his motivation. Even from across the country, Watkins keeps up with Abrielle’s softball exploits. She’s playing 13-and-under now. He bragged about her recently striking out three batters while pitching against older girls.
 He smiled in the 49ers locker room as he remembered competing with her. They’d pitch from the mound she’s got in the yard, see who could throw the most strikes. He’d laugh at her precocious moments, listen to her stories and play games.
 He sees himself in Abrielle. Her ambition. Her competitiveness. The hunger behind the wide smile. Even her occasional preteen stubbornness.
 “I try to call her and inspire her as much as possible,” he said. ‘Give her as much advice as I can. But, you know, being a kid, sometimes they don’t want to listen.”
 Thankfully for Watkins, some of the best lessons come without words.
 Including the one he taught the 49ers about him on Sunday. That his potential translates to production. He’s dependable even while he’s developing. That he’s going to come down with the ball.
 The 49ers could still trade for another receiver by Tuesday’s deadline. If not, Watkins made the kind of play that declares he’s ready for more. Especially until Evans and Samuel return. Finally, Watkins’ time is now.

 San Francisco's defense had five takeaways in the second half. "Just guys being in the right spot, doing their job, playing relentlessly." 
 New heights sometimes require new motivations. Watkins might’ve opened the door for the opportunity of a lifetime. Not just his own.
 His newest motivation is 2 years old.
 “Once I had my daughter, it kind of transformed into her,” Watkins said. “Just making sure I’m doing what I can do to be able to provide for her. (Make sure she doesn’t live) the lifestyle that I had growing up.”
 She celebrated her second birthday last week. Too young to revel in what happened Sunday. Too young to comprehend the stakes riding on him catching a ball from the sky. Or the sacrifices that made it possible.
 But she’s old enough to be his new purpose.
 The love of his little sister got him a long way. For what comes next, Watkins has something even stronger.
 Eyes that look like his own.
 A smile that washes away worry.
 And every reason in the world to come down with the ball.
 Correction: An earlier version of this article misstated that Ricky Pearsall was injured this season. It was last season. The article has been corrected.
